source.title: Data-efficient pre-training by scaling synthetic megadocs
source.authors: K. Kim; Suhas Kotha; Yejin Choi; Tatsunori Hashimoto; Nick Haber; Percy Liang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports loss and downstream results while scaling synthetic generations and using megadoc training recipes. This is a new training-data setting, not a reproduction of the parameter/token/compute sweeps in the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The study does not test power laws in parameter count, training tokens, or compute; extrapolation from small runs; a compute-optimal parameter/token split; or architecture sensitivity. Its own results on synthetic-generation scaling and associated downstream accuracy are recorded. Results attributed to cited studies, including the 1.3M-token self-improvement results in Appendix A.2, are not recorded as this study's results. Many plotted curves have no numerical values in the text and are not separately extracted.
record.test_reason: The study varies synthetic generations per document and document construction for a fixed 300M student and 200M real tokens. It does not vary parameters, tokens or compute to test a power law, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation or architecture shape. It uses a data-scaling law from Kim et al. (2025) as a tool to convert loss into 'data efficiency'. Its benchmark results report its own methods' gains over a baseline. The only link to V6 is a qualitative remark that benchmark trends match loss trends. The authors also say benchmark scaling looks 'less well-behaved', and they give no loss-to-accuracy fit. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that mixing synthetic rephrases with real data lowers i.i.d. web loss, monotonically in generation count. Megadocs (stitched rephrasing, latent thoughts) scale better, raising data efficiency from 1.48x to 1.80x, with a gap that widens with more generations. They attribute this mainly to longer training without overfitting. They also conclude that these synthetic methods compose with ensembling, unlike self-distillation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies synthetic generations per fixed real document, mixing and epoching, megadocument construction, and a limited student-size comparison. It does not reproduce the original parameter/token/compute scaling sweeps or the compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on synthetic-data method and hyperparameter tuning. Megadocs permit more real-data epochs and higher synthetic mixing fractions; when megadoc methods use simple-rephrasing hyperparameters to control for longer training, their advantage does not scale with generation count in the same way. The real document's placement in stitched sequences also changes loss.

fits_no_version.finding: With fixed real data, i.i.d. loss falls monotonically in synthetic generations per document. Simple rephrasing plateaus near 3.41 at 32 generations (baseline 3.55). Megadocs improve on this, and the gap widens from 0.02 to 0.07. Estimated data efficiency is 1.48x, 1.64x and 1.80x.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under fixed real data, loss can be lowered by scaling synthetic generations, with method-dependent plateaus.

fits_no_version.finding: The synthetic-data loss win over the real-data baseline is larger at 1.5B than at 300M, by at least 0.06, for all three methods. The 1.5B runs were not locally optimal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Synthetic-data gains from a fixed generator grow with student size in this setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Megadocs improve long-context validation loss on arXiv CS papers by 0.14 and 0.19 at 32 generations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Megadocument recipes improve long-context loss in the tested setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Ensemble loss falls as a power law in member count with exponent 1. Self-distilled ensembles reach the same asymptote as standard ones (3.32 vs 3.31). Synthetic-data ensembles lower the asymptote by at least 0.12.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensemble-count power-law asymptotes differ by data recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Average accuracy on PIQA, SciQ and ARC Easy rises by 5%, 6% and 9% over the real-data baseline, qualitatively tracking the loss gains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this setup, downstream accuracy gains from synthetic-data recipes follow their loss gains.

record.code_released: The paper says its code is open-source on GitHub; a code URL is not stated.
record.problems: The main experiments use one 200M-token dataset, a 300M student, and an external Llama 3.1 8B Instruct generator. The 1.5B ablations are explicitly not locally optimal. Many curve values are presented only in figures, and some reported loss improvements do not specify their comparison baseline. Data-efficiency values are estimates based on a scaling law from cited work.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only point values and detailed per-generation curve entries were not separately extracted because the text does not state their numeric values. Other figure-only comparisons, including the ensemble asymptote results in Figure 7 and validation-set comparisons in Figures 4, 5, 15, and 16, are not rows for the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No sweep over parameters, tokens or compute. There are only two student sizes, with no baseline losses stated.
No extrapolation from small fitted runs to larger runs.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in another modality or regime. The ensemble power law is in member count, not model scale.
No fit or test of downstream accuracy against scale or pretraining loss. There is only a qualitative statement that benchmark gains match loss gains.
No comparison of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label was removed. The benchmark rows report method gains over a baseline at fixed scale, not downstream predictability from scale or loss. The study uses a cited data-scaling law (Kim et al. 2025) only to translate losses into data-efficiency multiples, hence uses_without_test/T4.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation and its scaling with compute.
Loss sensitivity to depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form across other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures downstream accuracy for PIQA, SciQ, and ARC Easy under its synthetic-data recipes, but does not test general predictability across tasks, models, or scales.
It varies synthetic-data recipes and hyperparameters, but does not test whether published power-law exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices.
